title: 🔬 Science Lab: Sort & Discover
description: Welcome to the Science Lab! Sort elements into their periodic table groups, classify chemicals by their properties, and organize lab equipment by function. One wrong sort could cause a lab accident! Learn safety protocols while having fun.
learning_objectives: Distinguish between metals and non-metals based on their periodic table classification and properties
Identify common acids encountered in everyday life and laboratory settings
Understand the purpose and importance of essential lab safety equipment
Learn interesting scientific facts with real-world and India-relevant connections
Develop categorization and critical thinking skills through hands-on sorting

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Read each item's name and description carefully
Drag the item into the correct bucket: Metals, Non-Metals, Acids, or Lab Safety Equipment
Earn 15 points for each correct sort, but lose 5 points for wrong placements
Sort all 20 items to complete the lab session and see your final score
Read the fun facts after each sort to learn fascinating science trivia
tips: Metals are usually shiny, conduct electricity, and are found on the left side of the periodic table
Non-metals are often gases or brittle solids at room temperature and sit on the right side of the periodic table
Acids have a pH less than 7 and are often corrosive -- some are found in everyday foods!
Lab safety equipment protects you from chemical spills, fumes, and fire hazards -- always gear up before experimenting

buckets.name: Metals
buckets.description: Metallic elements -- shiny, conductive, malleable substances found on the left and centre of the periodic table

buckets.name: Non-Metals
buckets.description: Non-metallic elements -- often gases or brittle solids that are poor conductors, found on the right side of the periodic table

buckets.name: Acids
buckets.description: Acidic substances -- compounds with pH less than 7 that release hydrogen ions (H⁺) in solution

buckets.name: Lab Safety Equipment
buckets.description: Safety gear and tools -- essential protective equipment used in laboratories to prevent accidents and injuries

items.name: Iron (Fe)
items.fun_fact: India is the world's 2nd largest producer of crude steel. The Iron Pillar of Delhi, over 1,600 years old, has barely rusted -- a testament to ancient Indian metallurgy!

items.name: Copper (Cu)
items.fun_fact: Copper is an excellent conductor of electricity and is used in almost all electrical wiring. India's Khetri Copper Complex in Rajasthan is one of the country's major copper mining operations.

items.name: Gold (Au)
items.fun_fact: Gold is so malleable that a single gram can be beaten into a sheet of 1 square metre! India is one of the largest consumers of gold in the world, and the Kolar Gold Fields in Karnataka were historically among the deepest mines on Earth.

items.name: Aluminium (Al)
items.fun_fact: Aluminium is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust but is never found free in nature -- it must be extracted from bauxite ore. India has large bauxite reserves in Odisha and is among the top 10 aluminium producers globally.

items.name: Sodium (Na)
items.fun_fact: Sodium is a soft, silvery metal that reacts violently with water! India's Sambhar Lake in Rajasthan is the country's largest inland salt lake and a major source of sodium chloride (common salt).

items.name: Oxygen (O₂)
items.fun_fact: Oxygen makes up about 21% of Earth's atmosphere and is essential for respiration. During the COVID-19 pandemic, India massively scaled up its medical oxygen production capacity to meet the surge in demand.

items.name: Carbon (C)
items.fun_fact: Carbon can exist as both the hardest natural substance (diamond) and one of the softest (graphite). India is one of the world's leading diamond cutting and polishing centres, with Surat processing about 90% of the world's diamonds.

items.name: Nitrogen (N₂)
items.fun_fact: Nitrogen makes up 78% of Earth's atmosphere! It is essential for plant growth, and India's fertilizer industry (producing urea from nitrogen) is one of the largest in the world, supporting millions of farmers.

items.name: Sulphur (S)
items.fun_fact: Sulphur is a bright yellow non-metal with a distinctive smell. It is used in making matches, gunpowder, and medicines. The sulphur springs at Tapovan in Uttarakhand are famous for their hot, mineral-rich waters.

items.name: Chlorine (Cl₂)
items.fun_fact: Chlorine is a greenish-yellow toxic gas used widely for water purification. India's National Rural Drinking Water Programme uses chlorination to make water safe for millions of people across the country.

items.name: Hydrochloric Acid (HCl)
items.fun_fact: Hydrochloric acid is naturally produced in your stomach to help digest food! It has a pH of about 1-2 and is also known as muriatic acid, commonly used for cleaning and industrial processes in India.

items.name: Sulphuric Acid (H₂SO₄)
items.fun_fact: Sulphuric acid is called the 'King of Chemicals' because it is used in more industrial processes than any other chemical. India is among the top producers, and it is essential for manufacturing fertilizers, detergents, and car batteries.

items.name: Citric Acid
items.fun_fact: Citric acid is the tangy substance found in lemons, oranges, and amla (Indian gooseberry). India is a major global producer of citric acid, and nimbu paani (lemon water) is a beloved everyday drink across the country!

items.name: Acetic Acid (Vinegar)
items.fun_fact: Acetic acid gives vinegar its sour taste and pungent smell. In Indian cuisine, vinegar is a key ingredient in Goan dishes like vindaloo and in pickling achaar (Indian pickles) to preserve them for months!

items.name: Nitric Acid (HNO₃)
items.fun_fact: Nitric acid is a powerful oxidizing acid used in making fertilizers and explosives. India's fertilizer industry relies heavily on nitric acid to produce ammonium nitrate, which is vital for agriculture across the country.

items.name: Safety Goggles
items.fun_fact: Safety goggles protect your eyes from chemical splashes, flying particles, and harmful fumes. The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) sets strict safety standards for protective eyewear used in Indian laboratories and industries.

items.name: Fire Extinguisher
items.fun_fact: Different types of fire extinguishers are used for different fires -- water, CO₂, foam, and dry powder. In India, the National Building Code mandates fire extinguishers in all labs and public buildings for safety.

items.name: Fume Hood
items.fun_fact: A fume hood is a ventilated workspace that draws harmful gases and vapours away from the user. India's top research institutions like IISc Bangalore and IITs use advanced fume hoods to protect researchers working with toxic chemicals.

items.name: Lab Coat
items.fun_fact: Lab coats are made of cotton or special flame-resistant materials to protect your skin and clothing from chemical spills. The white colour makes it easy to spot any contamination quickly -- that is why scientists around the world wear them!

items.name: First Aid Kit
items.fun_fact: A lab first aid kit includes burn cream, eyewash solution, bandages, and antiseptic. India's Factories Act 1948 mandates that every workplace and laboratory must have a fully stocked first aid kit accessible to all workers.

glossary_terms.definition: A tabular arrangement of all known chemical elements organized by their atomic number, electron configuration, and recurring chemical properties. Created by Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869, it currently contains 118 confirmed elements.

A scale from 0 to 14 that measures how acidic or basic (alkaline) a substance is. A pH below 7 is acidic, exactly 7 is neutral (pure water), and above 7 is basic. Lemon juice has a pH of about 2, while soap is around 10.

A chemical reaction that releases energy in the form of heat or light to its surroundings. Examples include combustion (burning), mixing water with strong acids, and the setting of cement. The opposite is an endothermic reaction, which absorbs heat.

A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed or permanently changed in the process. Enzymes in your body are biological catalysts. For example, manganese dioxide (MnO₂) catalyses the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.

A simple chemical test using litmus paper (made from lichens) to determine whether a solution is acidic or basic. Blue litmus paper turns red in acid, and red litmus paper turns blue in a base. It is one of the oldest and most widely used pH indicators.

achievements.title: 🧫 Lab Apprentice
achievements.description: Sort all 20 items correctly and achieve a perfect score of 300 points
achievements.reward_message: Flawless sorting! You have the precision of a seasoned chemist. Every element, acid, and piece of safety gear is exactly where it belongs!

achievements.title: 🛡️ Safety First Champion
achievements.description: Correctly sort all 5 Lab Safety Equipment items without any mistakes
achievements.reward_message: You know your safety protocols inside and out! A safe lab is a productive lab. You are ready to handle any experiment responsibly.

achievements.title: ⚗️ Element Expert
achievements.description: Correctly sort all 10 elements (Metals and Non-Metals) without any mistakes
achievements.reward_message: Mendeleev would be proud! You can tell your metals from your non-metals like a true periodic table master. Keep exploring the elements!

cultural_context: Scientific literacy is a strategic priority under NEP 2020, which emphasises inquiry-based learning over rote memorisation. 🔬 Science Lab: Sort & Discover builds the analytical instincts that support strong performance in India's science curricula.
reflection_prompt: What pattern did you start to recognize as you played? How will you use it next time?
